knowledge:
- key_parameters: random_state=Integer seed (e.g., 42L) passed to fitsne to ensure reproducibility of the t-SNE embedding ;; new=Matrix of new data points to project into the existing embedding in project() ;; old=Matrix of original data points used to create the embedding in project()
- alternatives: openTSNE Python package (which this package wraps) ;; FI-tSNE algorithm by Linderman et al. (2018)
- when_to_use: Appropriate for dimensionality reduction of high-dimensional datasets (such as single-cell RNA-seq principal components) and when there is a need to map new query samples onto a pre-existing reference t-SNE visualization.
- pitfalls: t-SNE embeddings are stochastic and can be unstable, so it is good practice to run the algorithm multiple times to ensure robustness ;; Ensure random_state is specified as an integer (with L) for exact reproducibility.

workflows.name: run_fitsne
workflows.intent: Run fast interpolated t-SNE (FI-tSNE) on a high-dimensional matrix to generate 2D coordinates.
input: counts (a matrix of high-dimensional data, such as principal components or normalized gene expression counts, where rows are samples and columns are features)
workflows.stages: 1. Run FI-tSNE using the fitsne function ;; 2. Visualize the resulting 2D coordinates

workflows.name: project_new_data
workflows.intent: Project new, unseen test data into an existing t-SNE embedding.
input: train_mat (matrix of training data used to build the initial embedding)
test_mat (matrix of new test data to project into the embedding)
workflows.stages: 1. Generate the reference t-SNE embedding on training data using fitsne ;; 2. Project the new test data into the reference embedding using project
workflows.code:
embedding <- fitsne(train_mat, random_state = 42L)
new_coords <- project(embedding, new = test_mat, old = train_mat)
